side-to-side-blend.motion: Start with Clear sky blue across the top and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up Pale horizon blue and paint below it, down past where the trees and mountain go. Then stroke back up over the join several times.
side-to-side-blend.result: Smooth bands of blue, deeper at the top and paler low down, with a soft join where the two wet blues meet.
side-to-side-blend.then: Stroke back over the join while it's wet.

mistakes.mistake: A hard line where the two blues meet.
mistakes.fix: Add more Pale horizon blue at the join and blend again.
Wipe it on a rag. Rinse before going into white.

diagram.title: Blend the two sky blues side to side

curved-strokes.motion: Bend every stroke with the mountain: from the top of each peak down along its slope.
curved-strokes.result: Marks that run down the slopes, which is what makes the mountain look sloped.
curved-strokes.then: Use the darker mix along the shadow side and the lighter one along the lit side, both following the slopes.

diagram.title: Strokes that run down the slopes

stages.caption: Strokes down the slopes, lighter toward the light

dry-brush.motion: Light pressure, skimming over the rock and the right-hand slopes of the mountain.
dry-brush.result: Feathery, broken, see-through blue marks that catch the canvas texture on the shadow side. Never a solid area.
dry-brush.then: Build up in several light passes.

mistakes.mistake: The shadow went on as solid blue.
mistakes.fix: Let it dry, then dry-brush Light mountain blue back over part of it.

diagram.title: Skim the shadow on, with almost no paint

stages.caption: Light, broken strokes of lake blue

fan-tapping.motion: Stamp only the tips, using the middle of the fan, not the side bristles. For each spruce, work from its top point down in a zigzag and press harder as you go down, so it widens. Short strokes in different directions make the rough far woods.
fan-tapping.result: Clusters of fine, needle-like marks, light at each spruce's tip and heavier where pressed toward its base.
fan-tapping.then: If a spruce's top is too heavy, add a few fine lines with a small round instead of more fan marks.

mistakes.why: The paint is too thick, the bristles are clumped, or you stamped with the side.
mistakes.fix: Thin the paint a little, spread the fan, and stamp with the middle tips.

diagram.title: Tap the spruce's tip, then zigzag down

build-from-pieces.motion: Start with one simple shape: a rectangle for the walls. Then add the rest in pieces: the roof's triangle on top, and the gable end on the right.
build-from-pieces.result: A cabin made of distinct pieces, with small gaps or overlaps between them.
build-from-pieces.then: Leave the pieces showing: the shade and the roof go on them next.

horizontal-strokes.motion: Keep the brush level and the strokes long, left and right, across the whole lake.
horizontal-strokes.result: Flat, level bands of lake blue that seem to stretch away to the far shore, with slight streaks that follow the stroke.
horizontal-strokes.then: Lighter and smoother toward the far shore, darker and more textured in front.

stages.caption: A few darker streaks left in

pull-down.motion: Stroke straight down, starting just below the spruces at the waterline.
pull-down.result: Soft, streaky, see-through dark green marks straight down under the trees.
pull-down.then: Once dry, cross it with thin level dashes of the base color.

horizontal-dashes.motion: Short, level dashes across the forest's reflection. Small and close together near the far shore, longer and wider apart lower down.

mistakes.mistake: The dashes smear into the dark green reflection.
mistakes.fix: Paint them over a dry layer only.

stages.caption: Short and close at the top, longer below

x-stroke.motion: Short strokes that cross each other in two directions, like overlapping X shapes, filling the reed clump.
x-stroke.result: A soft, slightly textured dark green fill with visible criss-cross marks: the dark heart of the reeds.
x-stroke.then: Leave it as texture: the flicked blades go over it once it's dry.

diagram.title: Fill the clump with crossing strokes

flicking.motion: A quick stroke upward from the base of the reeds, lifting off as it goes, so each blade thins at the top.
flicking.result: Tapered blades with broken tips, denser at the base of the clump.
flicking.then: Flick a lighter green over the dark base, fewer as you go up, so the dark shows between the blades.

The streaks from steps 13 and 14 should still read as upside-down trees afterwards, only softer.

lines.text: Let the reflections and the lake dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 2 in from the bottom edge, and its left side is at the left edge; it's about 3 1/2 in wide and 4 in tall.
Paint: Dark reed green.
Brush: 1/2 inch flat. Load: One or two colors on the brush. Here it is Dark reed green alone, so load it evenly.
Short strokes that cross each other in two directions, like overlapping X shapes.
It should leave an even dark fill with a few criss-cross marks showing, its edges broken rather than smooth.

brushes.use: Lay in the dark reed clump

steps.reason: cut from the finish inside the part's outline
steps.summary: Block in the dark green base of the reed clump at the left edge of the lake.
steps.tip: The clump is about 3 1/2 in wide and 3 3/4 in tall, its left side at the left edge of the canvas, its top about 6 in from the top edge and its bottom about 2 in from the bottom edge. Give it a ragged top and a ragged right side, as the after picture shows, so the blades in steps 19 and 20 have a dark ground to rise from. Leave the olive reflection marks the before picture already shows in the water as they are.

lines.text: Let the reeds and the reflections dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 2 in from the bottom edge, and its left side is at the left edge; it's about 3 in wide and 4 in tall.
Paint: Mossy green.
Brush: fan brush. Load: A light load. Too much paint makes flat blobs.
A quick stroke upward from the base, lifting off as it goes, so each mark thins at the top.
It should leave tapered marks with broken tips, denser at the base.
Leave what step 18 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
Watch out: blades all the same height and evenly spaced look like a fence. Fix: mix short and tall blades, crowd them at the base, and let a few lean.

brushes.use: Flick in the mossy reed blades

steps.reason: cut from the finish inside the part's outline
steps.summary: Flick mossy green blades up from the base of the dark reed clump.
steps.tip: Most of what this step adds is in the bottom half of the reeds: the biggest group of blades has its left side at the left edge, its top about 8 in from the top edge, and is about 2 1/2 in wide and 2 in tall. A smaller group has its top about 6 in from the top edge and its left side about 1 1/4 in from the left edge, about 1 1/4 in wide and 1 1/2 in tall. Flick every blade upward from the base, some leaning a little, and keep the Dark reed green showing between them.

lines.text: Let the reeds and the reflections dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 2 in from the bottom edge, and its left side is at the left edge; it's about 3 1/2 in wide and 4 in tall.
Paint: Sunlit olive.
Brush: fan brush. Load: A light load. Too much paint makes flat blobs.
A quick stroke upward from the base, lifting off as it goes, so each mark thins at the top.
It should leave tapered marks with broken tips, denser at the base.
Leave what steps 18 and 19 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
Watch out: covering the whole clump in olive flattens it. Fix: keep gaps so the darker greens of steps 18 and 19 show between the light blades.
Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

brushes.use: Flick in the sunlit olive blades

steps.reason: cut from the finish inside the part's outline
steps.summary: Flick sunlit olive blades over the reed clump to catch the morning sun.
steps.tip: The sun comes from the upper left, so these blades are the sunlit ones; put the brightest where the after picture has them. The olive blades spread across the whole clump, about 3 1/2 in wide and 3 1/4 in tall, with the top of the group about 6 1/2 in from the top edge and its left side at the left edge. Flick each one upward from the base and let the Dark reed green and the Mossy green blades show between them, as the after picture shows.

lines.text: Let the reeds and the reflections dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
Optional: lightly chalk its outline first, from the transfer outline in Before you start, measuring from the canvas edges with a ruler.
Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is at the bottom edge, and its left side is at the left edge; it's about 6 in wide and 2 1/2 in tall.
Paint: Middle rock gray.
Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
Start with the biggest rounded rock at the left edge. Then add the rest as rounded pieces touching it, smaller and lower toward the right, like ( ).
It should leave one solid gray shape with a lumpy, bumpy top edge and no blue showing through the gray.

brushes.use: Block in the rocks in middle gray

steps.reason: cut from the finish inside the part's outline

construct.title: Build the rock pile from rounded lumps

stages.caption: Smaller ones beside it, tucked behind

steps.summary: Block in the shore rocks as one flat middle gray shape in the bottom left corner.
steps.tip: The shore rocks sit below the reeds, touching them, and reach the left edge and the bottom edge of the canvas: about 6 in wide and 2 1/2 in tall, with its top about 9 1/2 in from the top edge. Most of the shape is on the left side and in the bottom half, so its top edge is a row of lumpy bumps that drops lower toward the right side of the shore rocks, as the after picture shows.
paint_notes: If the blue underneath shows through the gray, let it dry and paint it twice.

lines.text: Let the shore rocks and the reflections dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is at the bottom edge, and its left side is at the left edge; it's about 6 in wide and 2 1/2 in tall.
Paint: Rock shadow gray.
Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
Bend every stroke with the shape: start under the rounded top of each rock and pull down along its curve to its base.
It should leave marks that bend with the shape, which is what makes it look round or sloped.
Leave what step 21 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.

brushes.use: Shade the rocks' undersides

steps.reason: cut from the finish inside the part's outline
steps.summary: Shade the bottoms and shadow sides of the shore rocks in dark gray.
steps.tip: The light comes from the upper left, so the shadow gray goes on the undersides of the rocks and the sides turned away from it, as the after picture shows. The biggest patch starts at the left edge with its top about 10 in from the top edge and is about 3 in wide; most of the shadow is in the bottom half of the shore rocks and on the left side.

lines.text: Let the shore rocks and the reeds dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is at the bottom edge, and its left side is at the left edge; it's about 6 in wide and 2 1/2 in tall.
Paint: Warm pale gray.
Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
Bend every stroke with the shape: from the top of each bump down along its curve, and around a round shape.
It should leave marks that bend with the shape, which is what makes it look round or sloped.
Leave what steps 21 and 22 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

brushes.use: Light the rocks' sunny tops

steps.reason: cut from the finish inside the part's outline
steps.summary: Light the sunny tops of the shore rocks in warm pale gray.
steps.tip: The light comes from the upper left, so the warm pale gray goes on the tops and left sides of the rocks, the faces turned toward it. The highest mark starts at the left edge with its top about 9 1/2 in from the top edge; most of the light is on the left side of the shore rocks. Keep it off the shadow gray at each rock's base so the rocks stay round.
